raw_evidence: on WhatsApp Share via Email A blue plaque has been unveiled at a Bowdon house to mark the life of William Wood, the social reformer known as “The Climbing Boys’ Friend” The plaque is at Willow Cottage, 28 Stamford Road, where Wood lived after retiring there in 1847. It was unveiled last week at a ceremony organised by Trafford Council’s Local Studies team, attended by residents, historians, council members, Connor Rand MP and the Friends of Bowd Wood, born in 1782, was a wool merchant who began campaigning in 1826 after seeing a young boy fall to his death inside a chimney onto a live fire. “Climbing boys” were children sent up chimneys to sweep them, often suffering burns, respiratory illness, deformity and suffocation From Bowdon he funded prosecutions against master sweeps who broke child labour laws, put up placards at railway stations and wrote to newspapers He also challenged magistrates and even Queen Victoria over the use of a child sweep at Windsor Castle His work with Lord Shaftesbury included testimony to the House of Lords in 1853, which helped lead to the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1875. Wood died in 1868, aged 85, seven years before the practice was banned. Six chimney sweeps from five towns carried his coffin to St Mary’s Churc

raw_evidence: New Manchester research suggests tackling the factors behind suspensions could help prevent repeated exclusions and support vulnerable pupils School suspensions are associated with a complex combination of socioeconomic disadvantage, special educational needs, peer relationships and pupils’ experiences of school, according to new research from The University of Manchester The study analysed survey responses from more than 19,000 secondary school pupils linked to administrative records across Hampshire & Isle of Wight, to examine a wide range of factors associated with whether pupils were suspended and how often suspensions occurred Researchers found pupils receiving special educational needs (SEN) support or with an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) were more than twice as likely to be suspended than pupils without SEN, while those eligible for free school meals were also at increased risk The analysis also identified a number of factors associated with lower suspension risk, including pupils feeling that they belonged at school, being satisfied with their academic attainment, having positive relationships with school staff and having stronger emotion regulation sk By contrast, higher levels of peer pressure, experiences of bullying, and recent substance use were associated with an increased likelihood of suspension

Emma Murray, 33, flew into a rage and threw the glass against a wall after accusing her partner of being unreceptive when she was telling him something. But the tumbler shattered on impact - sending a shard of glass into his face and causing a laceration to his eye Police called by Murray herself subsequently arrived at the scene and arrested her. When quizzed she said: ''I didn't mean for this to happen. I threw the glass out of frustration. [He] often does not listen to what I have to say.'' At Warrington Magistrates' Court Murray, of Laurel Walk in Partington , pleaded guilty to assault by beating and was fined £120 and ordered that she pay £133 in costs and surcharge. She had lived and died in Ancient Egypt 2,500 years before. Her coffin shows her to be a woman of status, and she died when she was around 50 to 60 years old Her body, in an open coffin, has been on almost continuous public display at Manchester Museum for two centuries. Millions know the museum as simply “the one with the mummies” But this morning the museum made a bombshell announcement: it’s taking her off display. The decision comes after a year-long public consultation, and is based on the museum’s understanding of what Asru’s wishes would have been Was this the right decision?
